# The writing on the wall

## Authors

- Henry R Bourne<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology University of California at San Francisco United States . He blogs about the challenges and opportunities associated with biomedical research at biomedwatch.wordpress.com . His research was supported by the NIH from 1969 to 2008, and he served as a reviewer of grant applications at intervals during this period. henry.bourne@ucsf.edu

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The biomedical research enterprise in the US has become unsustainable and urgent action is needed to address a variety of problems, including a lack of innovation, an over-reliance on soft money for faculty salaries, the use of graduate students as a source of cheap labour, and a ‘holding tank’ full of talented postdocs with limited career opportunities.

## The roots of the problem

Even the principal investigators and the institutions must now suspect that, despite their protests and fervent pleas for more money, funding for biomedical research in the US is going to contract significantly over the near term, and probably longer. They blame their present troubles—specifically, almost a decade of flat-lined NIH budgets—on Congressional gridlock and a weak economy when, in fact, they should share responsibility for creating an even more serious problem as a result of their actions and decisions over the past four decades. The annual budget of the NIH increased significantly over this period, rising from $1.06 billion in 1970 to $28.6 billion in 2005: annual growth averaged about 9% between 1970 and 1998, and was close to 15% during the subsequent five ‘doubling’ years (Korn et al., 2002). Well before the century turned, therefore, the biomedical research enterprise in the US had become addicted to expansion. Competition-driven feedback loops led institutions to hire more investigators, build more labs, make faculty salaries more dependent on NIH dollars (‘soft’ money), and attract more trainees to do the work—thus driving even fiercer competition among institutions and scientists.

The idea that excessive competition can block progress appears counterintuitive to many, but analysis of biomedical research funding shows this is the case (Teitelbaum, 2008; Stephan, 2011). Competition drives scientific discovery, but too much competition for scarce resources can block progress, and has done so. Thus, the growing flood of grant applications surpasses growth in NIH dollars, reduces the proportion of grants that are funded, and renders peer review increasingly arbitrary because a project ranked in the 20th percentile is often no less meritorious than one ranked in the 10th percentile (Berg, 2013).

Another problem is that we now have a ‘holding tank' of postdoctoral scholars that is overflowing with bright young scientists who are indentured to greying lab chiefs and are thus unable to break new ground as independent researchers (Bourne, 2012). The worst consequence, but harder to quantify, is that scientists avoid risky, creative projects in favour of ‘sure things’ more likely to be funded by conservative reviewers (Nicholson and Ioannidis, 2012).

The NIH appointed a Biomedical Workforce Task Force to propose how to deal with some of these problems. Although the task force appeared to recognize that the biomedical research enterprise in the US is not presently sustainable, its recommendations and the NIH's actions (so far) failed to grapple with the excessive dependence of research faculty salaries on grants, the need to separate the funding of graduate trainees from the funding of research, or the postdoc holding tank (Biomedical Workforce Task Force, 2012).

## Six questions and my answers to them

So what do the stakeholders in biomedical research in the US need to do? In my opinion they must unite to craft strategies that nourish the best young scientists, to prune less creative projects, and to make biomedical research able to sustain itself. Achieving this will require the stakeholders to answer a number of difficult questions. Below I list six of these questions, along with my answers to them.

### How can we reduce the growing reliance on soft-money PI salaries?

Medical schools and research institutes routinely rely on NIH research project grants to pay large proportions of PI salaries—a practice that is also beginning to afflict research universities. Soft money salaries weaken collegial bonds among scholars, make researchers less willing to teach, undermine loyalties of faculty and institutions to one another, and discourage innovation by PIs. The faintest whisper of curtailing soft-money salaries strikes terror into financially threatened academic institutions, but they would be well advised to put more of their own skin into the research game. Institutions should join PIs and the NIH to schedule gradual but substantial change. At first, perhaps, no faculty investigator should receive more than 90% of their salary from research project grants; if the bar were raised 10% every five years thereafter, within 20 years no PI would receive more than 50% of their salary from grants.

### How can we revise federal ‘indirect cost’ rules that reward behaviour that is not sustainable?

Innovative research depends more on good ideas, which generally come from PIs, than on laboratory bricks and mortar. However, the rules on reclaiming indirect costs on grants from the NIH and other federal agencies reward institutions for diverting funds that could be used to pay PI salaries into building new laboratories instead. The diversion reflects two problems (Alberts, 2010): (i) when an institution uses its own money to pay the salary of a PI, this is not counted as a ‘direct’ cost of research, so the institution can claim less for indirect costs from the NIH than they can when the salary of the PI is paid from the grant; (ii) institutions can reclaim certain indirect costs related to the construction of new buildings and laboratories. Until these rules are changed, research institutions would be crazy not to invest scarce funds in buildings rather than people.

### How can we stop paying PhD trainees from research project grants?

Institutions and PIs are recruiting more and more young PhD trainees as cheap labour for their labs, and paying their stipends from research project grants rather than training grants. This has three adverse consequences: first, floods of newly minted PhDs apply for postdoctoral positions and jobs in industry, in numbers that drive down their salaries in whatever job they can get; second, institutions track trainees paid from training grants, but they do a terrible job of tracking the very large number of trainees paid from research project grants, making it impossible to know their numbers and eventual fates (knowledge that is essential for regulating the numbers of PhDs and postdocs); third, although trained to a very high level in laboratory research, too many PhD graduates settle for jobs that do not involve research and may not even relate to science, thereby wasting trainee positions and research dollars (Biomedical Workforce Task Force, 2012). The NIH focuses on the third of these issues, but it appears to ignore the obvious remedy for all three: to support all PhD trainees on training grants, not research project grants. Making this change in a gradual manner would be possible, but not easy, if PIs and institutions cooperated with the NIH.

### How can we create a sustainable laboratory workforce?

The dangers of excessive competition among PIs and institutions, as described above, will intensify as long as training for young scientists (both graduate students and postdocs) is driven by the demand for cheap lab workers, rather than by sustainable increases in positions for new PIs. Thus it is crucial for labs to hire more staff scientists and fewer junior faculty supported primarily on grants, while maintaining a reduced but still substantial number of postdocs and young scientists in training positions. To promote such changes in laboratory personnel, PIs and institutions must work with the NIH to define both the roles and support mechanisms for staff scientists.

### How can we shrink the postdoc ‘holding-tank’?

This goal will also require concerted efforts of both institutes and the NIH to shorten postdoctoral service to a maximum of five years, to eliminate quasi-faculty slots that lack all institutional salary support, and to impose more stringent quality controls on entry of both US and foreign PhDs into the ‘tank’.

### How can we ensure the appropriate balance between investigator-driven research into fundamental biological mechanisms, ‘big science’ and translational projects?

The size and complexity of the NIH make it difficult to even identify and quantify how much is spent on these three areas, and it is even harder to compare them in terms of ‘bangs for your buck’. There is a vast literature on this topic but, so far as I can see, very little meaningful data. Along with many colleagues, however, I strongly suspect that current trends at NIH dangerously limit its investment in research aimed at explaining fundamental biological mechanisms. All stakeholders in biomedical research must work together to resolve these issues, relying less on pontification (by me and everyone else, whatever their opinions) and more on data and critical analysis.

## Cooperation is required

Why do universities and PIs remain silent on questions that affect sustainability of their cherished research enterprise? Rather than sheer stupidity, I suspect the answer is blind arrogance: they fondly imagine that more vulnerable competitors will succumb to the current financial scourge, allowing the stronger, brighter dinosaurs (that is, themselves) to slither from their bunkers and garner whatever resources remain. Bunkers may suffice for a while, but even a thunder lizard can't survive long on magic alone. Instead, the changes needed to sustain biomedical research require hard thinking and cooperation among all biomedical research stakeholders. The NIH cannot solve the problems by itself. Researchers should argue strongly for sustained federal support, but it is delusional to expect a return to the era of regular 9% annual funding increases. We need no prophets to read the writing on the wall. Instead, for the foreseeable future, we must all sustain the enterprise with what we can get.

claims.source: Along with many colleagues, however, I strongly suspect that current trends at NIH dangerously limit its investment in research aimed at explaining fundamental biological mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative concern shared by the author and colleagues.

claims.claim: All stakeholders in biomedical research must work together to resolve issues of research balance, relying less on pontification and more on data and critical analysis.
claims.source: All stakeholders in biomedical research must work together to resolve these issues, relying less on pontification (by me and everyone else, whatever their opinions) and more on data and critical analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for how to address the problem.

claims.claim: Universities and PIs imagine that more vulnerable competitors will succumb to the current financial scourge, allowing the stronger, brighter dinosaurs to slither from their bunkers and garner whatever resources remain.
claims.source: Rather than sheer stupidity, I suspect the answer is blind arrogance: they fondly imagine that more vulnerable competitors will succumb to the current financial scourge, allowing the stronger, brighter dinosaurs (that is, themselves) to slither from their bunkers and garner whatever resources remain.
claims.evidence: This is the author's speculation about the motivations of universities and PIs.

claims.claim: The changes needed to sustain biomedical research require hard thinking and cooperation among all biomedical research stakeholders.
claims.source: Instead, the changes needed to sustain biomedical research require hard thinking and cooperation among all biomedical research stakeholders.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about what is required to address the problems.

claims.claim: The NIH cannot solve the problems by itself.
claims.source: The NIH cannot solve the problems by itself.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of NIH action alone.

claims.claim: It is delusional to expect a return to the era of regular 9% annual funding increases.
claims.source: Researchers should argue strongly for sustained federal support, but it is delusional to expect a return to the era of regular 9% annual funding increases.
claims.evidence: This is an evaluative claim about future funding expectations.

claims.claim: For the foreseeable future, we must all sustain the enterprise with what we can get.
claims.source: Instead, for the foreseeable future, we must all sustain the enterprise with what we can get.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding recommendation about adapting to resource constraints.

claims.claim: Principal investigators and institutions should share responsibility for creating the current problems in biomedical research.
claims.source: They blame their present troubles—specifically, almost a decade of flat-lined NIH budgets—on Congressional gridlock and a weak economy when, in fact, they should share responsibility for creating an even more serious problem as a result of their actions and decisions over the past four decades.
claims.evidence: This is an evaluative claim about responsibility for the current situation.

claims.claim: There has been almost a decade of flat-lined NIH budgets.
claims.source: They blame their present troubles—specifically, almost a decade of flat-lined NIH budgets—on Congressional gridlock and a weak economy when, in fact, they should share responsibility for creating an even more serious problem as a result of their actions and decisions over the past four decades.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about recent NIH budget trends.

claims.claim: No faculty investigator should receive more than 90% of their salary from research project grants at first, with the bar raised 10% every five years thereafter.
claims.source: At first, perhaps, no faculty investigator should receive more than 90% of their salary from research project grants; if the bar were raised 10% every five years thereafter, within 20 years no PI would receive more than 50% of their salary from grants.
claims.evidence: This is a specific policy recommendation with a gradual implementation plan.

claims.claim: Within 20 years of implementing the proposed salary policy, no PI would receive more than 50% of their salary from grants.
claims.source: At first, perhaps, no faculty investigator should receive more than 90% of their salary from research project grants; if the bar were raised 10% every five years thereafter, within 20 years no PI would receive more than 50% of their salary from grants.
claims.evidence: This is a projected outcome of the proposed policy based on arithmetic calculation.

claims.claim: Institutions should join PIs and the NIH to schedule gradual but substantial change in soft-money salary practices.
claims.source: Institutions should join PIs and the NIH to schedule gradual but substantial change.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for collaborative action.

claims.claim: The faintest whisper of curtailing soft-money salaries strikes terror into financially threatened academic institutions.
claims.source: The faintest whisper of curtailing soft-money salaries strikes terror into financially threatened academic institutions, but they would be well advised to put more of their own skin into the research game.
claims.evidence: This describes the reaction of institutions to proposed changes, based on observation.

claims.claim: Academic institutions would be well advised to put more of their own skin into the research game.
claims.source: The faintest whisper of curtailing soft-money salaries strikes terror into financially threatened academic institutions, but they would be well advised to put more of their own skin into the research game.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for institutional behavior change.

results.result: NIH budget grew from $1.06 billion in 1970 to $28.6 billion in 2005, averaging 9% annual growth (1970-1998) and 15% during the doubling years (1998-2003), followed by nearly a decade of flat-lined budgets.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 provide specific budget figures with citation support (Korn et al., 2002), and C69 describes the subsequent flat-lining period. These are factual statements about NIH budget history that can be verified from public records and are appropriately cited.

results.result: The biomedical research enterprise became addicted to expansion before 2000, with competition-driven feedback loops causing institutions to hire more investigators, build more labs, increase soft money dependence, and attract more trainees, thereby intensifying competition. PIs and institutions share responsibility for creating these problems.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C68 present a causal narrative about institutional behavior based on inference rather than empirical evidence. While the budget growth data (C7-C9) is factual, the characterization of institutional responses as 'addiction' and the specific causal mechanisms described lack direct empirical support or quantitative evidence of these behavioral patterns.

results.result: Excessive competition blocks progress in biomedical research by increasing grant applications beyond funding capacity, reducing funding rates, making peer review arbitrary (with 20th percentile projects often as meritorious as 10th percentile), and causing scientists to avoid risky projects in favor of safe ones.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by citations (Teitelbaum, 2008; Stephan, 2011; Berg, 2013; Nicholson and Ioannidis, 2012). The logical chain from increased applications (C15) to reduced funding rates (C16) to arbitrary review (C17-C18) to risk-averse behavior (C21) is coherent and supported by cited analyses. The claim about percentile rankings (C18) is specifically cited to Berg, 2013.

results.result: There exists a 'holding tank' of postdoctoral scholars overflowing with talented young scientists who are indentured to senior lab chiefs and unable to pursue independent research, representing limited career opportunities.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 and C5 describe the postdoc problem with citation support (Bourne, 2012). While the metaphorical language ('holding tank,' 'indentured') is evaluative, the underlying issue of postdocs with limited career advancement opportunities is a documented phenomenon in the biomedical workforce literature.

results.result: Medical schools and research institutes routinely rely on NIH grants to pay large proportions of PI salaries (soft money), a practice spreading to research universities. This weakens collegial bonds, reduces teaching willingness, undermines institutional loyalty, and discourages innovation.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 about the prevalence of soft money salaries is stated as common knowledge but lacks quantitative data or citations. Claims C29-C32 about the consequences of soft money are presented as inferences without empirical evidence. While these effects are plausible, no studies or data are provided to demonstrate these specific causal relationships.

results.result: Federal indirect cost rules create perverse incentives by not counting institutional PI salary contributions as direct costs (reducing claimable indirect costs) while allowing institutions to reclaim indirect costs for building construction, thereby rewarding investment in infrastructure over people.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 describe specific provisions of federal indirect cost rules with citation support (Alberts, 2010). The mechanism by which these rules create incentives for building over salary support is clearly explained and represents a verifiable aspect of federal grant policy.

results.result: Institutions increasingly recruit PhD trainees as cheap labor, paying them from research grants rather than training grants. This causes oversupply that depresses salaries (C40), poor tracking of trainee outcomes (C42-C43), and waste when PhDs take non-research jobs (C45-C46).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 and C4 describe a trend without quantitative evidence. Claim C40 about salary depression is economic reasoning without data. Claims C42-C43 about poor tracking are assertions without evidence. Claims C45-C46 are supported by citation (Biomedical Workforce Task Force, 2012) but the characterization as 'waste' is evaluative. The overall result lacks sufficient empirical support for the claimed trends and consequences.

results.result: The NIH Biomedical Workforce Task Force recognized the unsustainability of the biomedical research enterprise but failed to address excessive salary dependence on grants, separation of trainee funding from research funding, or the postdoc holding tank.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 is factual. Claims C23-C26 represent the author's critical assessment of the Task Force report with citation (Biomedical Workforce Task Force, 2012). This is a verifiable evaluation based on the actual content (or lack thereof) in the Task Force recommendations regarding these specific issues.

results.result: The NIH focuses on PhD job placement issues but ignores the remedy of supporting all PhD trainees on training grants rather than research grants. This change would be possible but not easy with cooperation from PIs and institutions.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is a critical assessment of NIH priorities. Claim C48 presents this as an 'obvious remedy' without evidence that it would actually solve the stated problems. Claim C49 acknowledges implementation challenges but provides no analysis of feasibility, costs, or potential unintended consequences. This is primarily speculation presented as solution.

results.result: A proposed policy would cap PI salary from grants at 90% initially, increasing by 10% every five years to reach 50% maximum within 20 years. Institutions should cooperate despite resistance to invest more institutional funds in research.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 present a specific policy proposal with arithmetic projections but no analysis of feasibility, economic impact, or potential consequences. Claim C73 describes institutional resistance anecdotally. Claims C72 and C74 are recommendations without supporting analysis. This is speculation about policy solutions without evidence of effectiveness or implementability.

results.result: Competition dangers will intensify while training is driven by demand for cheap labor rather than sustainable PI positions. Labs should hire more staff scientists and fewer grant-dependent junior faculty while maintaining reduced trainee numbers, with stakeholders defining staff scientist roles and support.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is predictive speculation. Claims C51-C53 are recommendations without evidence that this workforce restructuring would solve the stated problems or analysis of implementation barriers, costs, or career path implications for staff scientists versus traditional academic tracks.

results.result: Shrinking the postdoc holding tank requires limiting postdocs to five years maximum, eliminating quasi-faculty positions without institutional salary support, and imposing stricter quality controls on PhD entry into postdoctoral positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 present policy recommendations without evidence of effectiveness, analysis of implementation mechanisms, or consideration of potential negative consequences (e.g., impact on international scientific collaboration, career flexibility, or research productivity). These are speculative solutions without supporting data.

results.result: NIH's size and complexity make it difficult to quantify spending on investigator-driven research, big science, and translational projects or compare their value. Despite vast literature, there is little meaningful data. The author suspects NIH dangerously limits investment in fundamental biological mechanisms research.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 accurately describe analytical challenges and literature gaps. Claim C61 is explicitly presented as speculation ('strongly suspect') shared with colleagues. Claim C62's call for data-driven analysis is appropriate given the acknowledged lack of meaningful data. The author appropriately qualifies the speculative nature of these claims.

results.result: The biomedical research enterprise is unsustainable with lack of innovation, and funding will likely contract. Universities and PIs remain silent due to competitive arrogance. Solutions require stakeholder cooperation; NIH alone cannot solve problems, and expecting return to 9% annual growth is delusional.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is the central thesis but relies on the supporting claims, many of which are uncertain. Claim C2 about lack of innovation is asserted without evidence. Claim C6 is speculation about future funding. Claim C63 about motivations is speculation. Claims C64-C67 are reasonable conclusions about need for cooperation but don't constitute empirical results. The overall sustainability claim lacks sufficient quantitative evidence.

results.result: Innovative research depends more on good ideas from PIs than on laboratory infrastructure.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 present value judgments about sources of innovation without empirical evidence. While this may reflect common beliefs in the research community, no data or studies are provided to support the claim that ideas matter more than infrastructure, or that PIs are the primary source of innovative ideas (versus trainees, staff, or collaborative teams).
